[moved from Dustin's personal repo to public stan-dev group]

see below.

> On Mar 1, 2016, at 3:39 PM, bgoodri <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> On Tue, Mar 1, 2016 at 3:34 PM, Bob Carpenter <notifi...@github.com>
> wrote:
>
> > Is the idea to bypass Stan C++ and RStan and write GMO
> > directly into RStanArm?
> >
>
> No, Dustin / Andrew is planning for gmo() / gmo_lmer() / gmo_glmer() to be
> separate from rstanarm, but I am planning to have gmo be one of the
> algorithms available for users to choose for rstanarm. But I still think
> the algorithm should be part of Stan or failing that rstan. It is not
> really different from optimizing() or vb() from the UI perspective.

I agree that it should be coded in Stan in C++.  I thought you
guys were all still working on the design --- at least Andrew tells
me it's premature for me to worry about this as it's just experimental.

So if that's still the case and all this discussion isn't about something
we're going to release any time soon, I'll go back to my regularly scheduled
day.

> > Can't you just take the fixed values and pass them into
> > log_prob as parameters and then ignore the resulting
> > gradients? It won't be as efficient as doing this all
> > the right way, but it should work and it probably won't be
> > any less efficient than what you're doing now by reconsituting
> > an entire model's data + fixed parameters.
> >
>
> Maybe.

If someone can lay out the API calls required from the model, we
can talk about updating the generated code to make it more
efficient.  It seems unlikely we're going to want to manage two
separately compiled Stan models in a Stan C++ implementation.

- Bob

[Cross-posted to stan-dev]

Thanks for the detailed comments.

Could someone who understands this Wiener thing please respond
on stan-users?

I've never understood the function or its doc and we get a steady

have been due to poor doc, not buggy code.

The next step would be to create reproducible errors.

- Bob

> On Feb 19, 2016, at 8:15 AM, Maciej Swat <macie...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi all
>
> I have a related comment.
> There are three potential typos in the STAN manual (2.9.0) in the
> PDF for 'Wiener Diffusion Model Distributions’, but I’m not sure if these
> bugs 2&3 proliferated into the code.
>
> 1. y is defined as 'y \in (0, \tau)’ but it should be 'y \in (\tau, \infty)’
> otherwise the term \sqrt{y - \tau} is undefined.
>
>
> Two others based on reference paper (Blurton et at. 2012)
>
> 2. the exponent of the denominator (y - \tau) should be 3/2 instead of 3
> See attached PDF plots for
> alphaB=3.25;tauB=0.25;betaB=0.4;deltaB=0.65; N = 150;
>
> 3. the numerator in standard normal distribution function \phi reads
> ‘(2k + \beta) \alpha’ instead of '2k + \alpha \beta’.
> The difference between these two results in very minor changes.
>
> Best Regards, Maciej
>

In the case of (a) it may be quite important to capture speed-accuracy manipulations in experiments.  It's my understanding that this is an important/defining aspect of the diffusion decision model (DDM), hence am I missing something here or is this mirrored application (e.g., as in two conjugate inverse gaussians)  capturing this important aspect of the data when we fit by this implementation?

messages.body_plain:
I'm curious, what are the reasons for keeping gmo_(g)lmer entirely separate from stan_(g)lmer? For the version of GMO where the user passes in their own Stan program(s) we won't have an equivalent in rstanarm,  but for the lmer and glmer style models I think having both gmo_(g)lmer and GMO support for stan_(g)lmer will be confusing for users and add unnecessary work in that both sets of functions would need to be maintained (including providing support for users).

Jonah

My hope with this would be to be able to perform nasty ODE integration (or any other expensive operation) in parallel over multiple threads.

So given AD calculations can be split into many independent and nested blocks, could one hope to have a chance to parallelize AD over threads then?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: stan_lasso
messages.body_plain:
So, we’ve been having some discussion about lasso in Stan and I wanted to give some perspective.

Lasso is, I would say, three things:
(1) Autotuned hierarchical regression that shrinks most coefficients close to 0.
(2) Regularized regression that shrinks most coefficients all the way to 0.
(3) Bayesian regression with a double-exponential prior (or, equivalently, L1-penalized likelihood).

I was saying we should have stan_lasso because lasso is a useful tool.  We should have something just as easy to use, that a user can just grab and run, something named stan_lasso (because the name is part of the game).

Our stan_lasso will be better and worse than standard lasso.  It will be better in two ways:  (a) full Bayes, will automatically account for uncertainty, (b) flexibility, it can be put into any Stan model, a user can add mesurement-error models, hierarchical structures, mixtures, etc etc etc.  It will be worse in two ways:  (a) slower, I assume, since Stan’s not optimized for this particular class of problems, (b) full Bayes version doesn’t shrink estimates all the way to zero (we might like that, but for most users this will be a drawback).

One question, as always with these Stan extensions, is how much we want to mimic the existing behavior of lasso and how much do we want to do our own thing?  A pure lasso emulator would be nearly pointless—but not completely, as it could be used as a component in larger Stan models.

With that all said, I can imagine different options:

- A stan_lasso function that fits a hierarchical model with double-exponential model and with other models being allowed also.  It’s now set up so we can do full Bayes.  Once we have GMO, we could have it do something very close to what is done by the official “lasso” function.

- Full Bayes with an option to shrink to 0 during post-processing.  I’m not quite sure how we would do this but I don’t think it would be hard to come up with something.

I think it’s ok if our default “lasso” function uses Aki’s preferred prior, if we have some option that pulls point estimates all the way to 0.  The point is that (1) the function should usable as a routine tool for regression with lots of predictors, (2) users can get that shrinkage-all-the-way-to-zero if that’s what they want, and (3) the double-exponential prior should be an option.

In any case, I do want a stan_lasso function, I don’t just want to send people to stan_glmer and have them navigate the options.
A

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, March 3, 2016 at 9:13:29 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I was saying we should have stan_lasso because lasso is a useful tool.  We should have something just as easy to use, that a user can just grab and run, something named stan_lasso (because the name is part of the game).

I think that gets to a broader question of "Who is the target audience of a high-level interface such as rstanarm (or StataARM, etc.)?"
Your answer to that question has usually been "people who don't use R or are frustrated by R and just want a simple(r) way to do modeling who may not be overtly Bayesian". From that perspective your suggestions to have R functions like stan_logit or stan_lasso in rstanarm make some sense.
My answer to that question has always been "experienced R users who are interested in or at least curious about Bayesian inference", which is why for any model fitting function stan_foo(), foo() is an existing R function that experienced R users are already familiar with. From that perspective, there shouldn't be a function named stan_lasso() because there is no lasso() function in R. Trevor Hastie's package called lars has a lars() function that can be called with type = "lasso", which is the default, but there are other penalization schemes. Hastie et al.'s glmnet package has a glmnet() function that takes a family argument and does lasso penalization by default. Conceivably, we could have a stan_glmnet() function that just calls stan_glm() with Laplace priors.

So, it is more that I am unconvinced by your answer to this broader question than I am by the specific application of it to lasso. But specifically
I don't think there are so many machine learning people who are itching to do Bayesian inference
I think machine learning people tend to prefer Matlab, Python, Julia, etc. over R

If there are a non-negligible number of machine learning people using R who are interested in or at least curious about Bayesian inference, then it is critically important to make sure that crowd understands
The penalty functions that they are familiar with are usually kernels of some prior.
The popular penalty functions are chosen to make finding the mode of the penalized likelihood function an easy optimization problem, but if mode-finding is not the goal, then you are free to choose a penalty / prior that makes more sense.

To reinforce those concepts, I think it makes sense to have the penalty / prior be a function argument that goes with a variety of likelihood functions rather than having the penalty / prior be part of the function name. That is why most of the models in rstanarm have an option for prior = hs() or prior = hs_plus() for hierarchical shrinkage, which works even if your outcome is binary, count, etc. Suppose someone wants to do L1-regularization when the outcome is binary, would you have them call stan_logit_lasso()?

> With that all said, I can imagine different options:
>
> - A stan_lasso function that fits a hierarchical model with double-exponential model and with other models being allowed also.  It’s now set up so we can do full Bayes.  Once we have GMO, we could have it do something very close to what is done by the official “lasso” function.
>
> - Full Bayes with an option to shrink to 0 during post-processing.  I’m not quite sure how we would do this but I don’t think it would be hard to come up with something.
>
> I think it’s ok if our default “lasso” function uses Aki’s preferred prior, if we have some option that pulls point estimates all the way to 0.  The point is that (1) the function should usable as a routine tool for regression with lots of predictors, (2) users can get that shrinkage-all-the-way-to-zero if that’s what they want, and (3) the double-exponential prior should be an option.

I think the word "lasso" is so associated with "L1-penalization" rather than "regularization" that it would be confusing to reassociate "lasso" with "regularization" generally or "hiearchical shrinkage priors" specifically. I would like to implement the projection method for selecting a subspace of a model, but to me, that would be a separate post-estimation function that works on anything estimated in rstanarm rather than calling stan_lasso(*, shrunk = TRUE).

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Bob — why are we trying to leech onto the popularity
of the LASSO when it is fundamentally frequentist?  Any appeal
we make to that community can only be accepted with so much
success as we’re ultimately trying to solve different problems.  If
you think there are secret (or potential) Bayesians hiding in those
ranks then I don’t think this will be all that helpful, either.  It would
be better to communicate the weaknesses of the LASSO and the
benefits of alternatives, rather than trying to bait and switch.

I also agree with Ben that we shouldn’t convolve everything the
LASSO actually does with just “regularization”.  If model projection
is desired it’s best to make that a post processing step that can be
done for anything rather than a separate R package for a few
models that will drain waaaaaaaay too much developer time.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan_lasso
messages.body_plain:
Although I like the identification of the core idea and its clear separation for further improvements (as I generally do with Andrew’s redefinitions), I agree with everyone else in not misusing the term “lasso”. This is the same complaint I had with the EP paper. I also agree with Ben’s summary of target audiences. Most likely the ones this would appeal to would be statisticians and machine learning R users who are curious about Bayesian inference.

But I think that it does make sense to have some standalone function, stan_something(), which by default (note: a minimal # of arguments need to be written) does a similar behavior as glmnet/lasso but “better” and just as fast. Right now, the user has to be pretty familiar with the behavior of various priors to use rstanarm.

> I agree with Bob — why are we trying to leech onto the popularity
> of the LASSO when it is fundamentally frequentist?

I think we can always be purists about things but practically we often need to make compromises about computation, whether it be to excite other communities or just to apply as Bayesians ourselves. That’s part of why we have ADVI, Laplace, and soon GMO for the “efficiency frontier” in inference, and also rstanarm for modeling convenience. For something like rstanarm, people may as well have just gone and defined Stan models but they chose to use R formulas instead; therefore it makes sense to also make it easy to specify sparse shrinkage-inducing type of parameter estimation.

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
I’m not going to harp on the importance of quantifying the accuracy of
all of these approximations, and the prematurity of trying to shove
them onto users, again, but that is not the most important point at
issue here which Bob has been consistently making.

The problem is that all of these features cost huge amounts of time
to build, test, and _maintain_.  They are not free and they are not
one off costs.  We are barely keeping up with what we have, let
alone getting to the long list of features we already want to implement
that have been motivated by our practical work.

This is as much a question of priorities as it is validity.

messages.subject: granularity of pull requests (was Re: [math] Feature/issue 202 vectorize all (#240))
messages.subject_clean: granularity of pull requests (was Re: [math] Feature/issue 202 vectorize all (#240))
messages.body_plain:
[issue discussion spinning out to stan-dev]

The issue of how granular we should make pull requests keeps
coming up. But we have competing goals. On the one hand, a pull
request should be a complete unit of functionality.  On the other
hand, it should be small, so that it's relatively easy to review.

We've been having a discussion on this particular Math lib issue,
but we don't have a general resolution.  I was proposing we put
in the pull request for the infrastructure, then follow it up
with pull requests for applications (in this case, the infrastructure
is all the template programs to do vectorization and the application
is the vectorization of our unary functions).

The vectorization of unary functions can then itself be in two stages.
One to update the math lib, another to add them to the Stan language.

That's what I propose, but what do other people think in terms of
granularity of pull requests?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
messages.body_plain:
Possible, but a major undertaking.  The key work will be
in synchronizing updates to the single autodiff tree from
the asynchronous parallel workers and figuring out how to
indicate in a model what can be done in parallel.  So we'd
need someone who understands threading.

Given that in our standard use case (researcher on desktop
or notebook running 4 chains) we're out of parallel computing
power.  So we've never prioritized multithreading.

C++11 won't be available until we can get it working for
all of our platforms and interfaces.  As soon as the RStan
and PyStan developers give us the sign off and we can get
Windows building C++11, we can move over.  I'd love to have
C++11 tools.  And I'm afraid Eigen and Boost are going there
without us anyway.

- Bob

As we already have boost anyway, we could consider boost threads, right? To my understanding boost threads works accross all platforms, it just uses a different implementation on windows/non-windows.
>
> The only caveat with it is that boost threads depends on some parts being build as a library, but this means that one would need to figure out a smart makefile for this which seems doable (given that we managed sundials/CVODE).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan_lasso
messages.body_plain:
If I may reiterate — the overall problem here is that developing ideas and
even algorithms is fast, but designing interfaces for those algorithms,
implementing them, and then testing and maintaining them is much slower.
So assume that every new feature will take 6-12 months, even if it took just
a few days to invent.

Now the problem comes about when ideas are being proposed at every
meeting.  We spend one or two weeks trying to figure out how to implement
the old feature and then all of the sudden it becomes deprecated by the
new feature.  Those weeks are then wasted, we have to start thinking about
something else, and nothing ever gets done.  It’s demotivating and frankly
demoralizing.  Software development, the kind that makes packages like
Stan _relatively_ pleasant experiences of users, evolves way more slowly
that the typical NIPS-style publication cycle.

WAIC and LOO were much more successful because in having to write the
paper you had to build and document prototypes that suggested interfaces
that could readily be turned into production code.  Also prototypes came
with lots of examples that were used for demonstration in the paper but
could be used at tests in the code.

In summary:

“I thought of this new algorithm, it’s neat.  Let me tell you about it so we
can discuss it.  I’m going to built a prototype, document a bunch of examples
of it working and maybe failing in a manuscript draft, and then let’s consider
adding it Stan.” is awesome and one of the most fun parts of working on
Stan.

“I thought of this new algorithm idea and haven’t prototyped it at all but it
should be in Stan.  Why isn’t it in Stan?  I _really_ want this in Stan now
guys.  Oh, hey, look at this new thing!  Let’s forget that old idea and focus
on this.” is where things becomes demotivating and demoralizing.

On Mar 4, 2016, at 12:52 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Understood.  I will start with the paper with example code and see how things go from there.  This is the path we took with Waic and LOO and it’s worked ok so far.
> A

>> of potatoes, five of blueberries, and a case of grapes in
>> wine form is too much to carry for one or two people.
>>
>> So we either buy a donkey or get choosy about which fruit
>> we tote around.
>>
>> - Bob

>>>
>>> Hi, if it’s too much to maintain, I can just write such functions myself with the help of Jonah, Aki, etc.  I think there is a real need for a function that has lasso-like behavior and I’d like it to be written using Stan so that it plays well with larger, more complicated models.
>>>
>>> One approach would be to start not with an R function but with a paper with some title such as Lasso-like Functionality Using Stan, that has example code demonstrating everything that I’d like to be doing.  The advantage of writing a paper with sample code is (a) it’s a paper, not a program, so it doesn’t have to be maintained, (b) people can take the sample code and adapt to their own problems, so we’re targeting the early adopters and power-users.
>>>

>>>>
>>>> I’m not going to harp on the importance of quantifying the accuracy of
>>>> all of these approximations, and the prematurity of trying to shove
>>>> them onto users, again, but that is not the most important point at
>>>> issue here which Bob has been consistently making.
>>>>
>>>> The problem is that all of these features cost huge amounts of time
>>>> to build, test, and _maintain_.  They are not free and they are not
>>>> one off costs.  We are barely keeping up with what we have, let
>>>> alone getting to the long list of features we already want to implement
>>>> that have been motivated by our practical work.
>>>>
>>>> This is as much a question of priorities as it is validity.
>>>>
>>>> On Mar 3, 2016, at 7:22 PM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> Although I like the identification of the core idea and its clear separation for further improvements (as I generally do with Andrew’s redefinitions), I agree with everyone else in not misusing the term “lasso”. This is the same complaint I had with the EP paper. I also agree with Ben’s summary of target audiences. Most likely the ones this would appeal to would be statisticians and machine learning R users who are curious about Bayesian inference.
>>>>>
>>>>> But I think that it does make sense to have some standalone function, stan_something(), which by default (note: a minimal # of arguments need to be written) does a similar behavior as glmnet/lasso but “better” and just as fast. Right now, the user has to be pretty familiar with the behavior of various priors to use rstanarm.
>>>>>
>>>>>> I agree with Bob — why are we trying to leech onto the popularity
>>>>>> of the LASSO when it is fundamentally frequentist?
>>>>>
>>>>> I think we can always be purists about things but practically we often need to make compromises about computation, whether it be to excite other communities or just to apply as Bayesians ourselves. That’s part of why we have ADVI, Laplace, and soon GMO for the “efficiency frontier” in inference, and also rstanarm for modeling convenience. For something like rstanarm, people may as well have just gone and defined Stan models but they chose to use R formulas instead; therefore it makes sense to also make it easy to specify sparse shrinkage-inducing type of parameter estimation.
>>>>>
>>>>> Dustin
>>>>>> On Mar 3, 2016, at 12:36 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>>>
>>>>>> I think this would be a terrible way to spend our limited
>>>>>> developer resources.  And I really hate the idea of trying
>>>>>> to co-opt the stupid name "lasso".
>>>>>>
>>>>>> - Bob
>>>>>>
>>>>>>
>>>>>>> On Mar 3, 2016, at 9:13 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> So, we’ve been having some discussion about lasso in Stan and I wanted to give some perspective.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Lasso is, I would say, three things:
>>>>>>> (1) Autotuned hierarchical regression that shrinks most coefficients close to 0.
>>>>>>> (2) Regularized regression that shrinks most coefficients all the way to 0.
>>>>>>> (3) Bayesian regression with a double-exponential prior (or, equivalently, L1-penalized likelihood).
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> I was saying we should have stan_lasso because lasso is a useful tool.  We should have something just as easy to use, that a user can just grab and run, something named stan_lasso (because the name is part of the game).
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> Our stan_lasso will be better and worse than standard lasso.  It will be better in two ways:  (a) full Bayes, will automatically account for uncertainty, (b) flexibility, it can be put into any Stan model, a user can add mesurement-error models, hierarchical structures, mixtures, etc etc etc.  It will be worse in two ways:  (a) slower, I assume, since Stan’s not optimized for this particular class of problems, (b) full Bayes version doesn’t shrink estimates all the way to zero (we might like that, but for most users this will be a drawback).
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> One question, as always with these Stan extensions, is how much we want to mimic the existing behavior of lasso and how much do we want to do our own thing?  A pure lasso emulator would be nearly pointless—but not completely, as it could be used as a component in larger Stan models.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> With that all said, I can imagine different options:
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> - A stan_lasso function that fits a hierarchical model with double-exponential model and with other models being allowed also.  It’s now set up so we can do full Bayes.  Once we have GMO, we could have it do something very close to what is done by the official “lasso” function.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> - Full Bayes with an option to shrink to 0 during post-processing.  I’m not quite sure how we would do this but I don’t think it would be hard to come up with something.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> I think it’s ok if our default “lasso” function uses Aki’s preferred prior, if we have some option that pulls point estimates all the way to 0.  The point is that (1) the function should usable as a routine tool for regression with lots of predictors, (2) users can get that shrinkage-all-the-way-to-zero if that’s what they want, and (3) the double-exponential prior should be an option.
>>>>>>>
>>>>>>> In any case, I do want a stan_lasso function, I don’t just want to send people to stan_glmer and have them navigate the options.
>>>>>>> A

messages.subject: Help with open issues on github.
messages.subject_clean: Help with open issues on github.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I could really use your help. There are way too many open issues on our repos and I really want it to be cut down to something reasonable.

Here is our current status:
- Stan: 218 open issues. https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues
- Stan Math: 112 open issues. https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues

If you have any time to spare, please help out. You don't have to be coder. You can do this with any 15 mins.

1. Go to either the Stan issues (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues) or Math issues (https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues) on GitHub. Log in.
2. Go to any page of the issues (preferably something older, but anywhere is good). Click on any issue. It'll look like this: https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/61
3. Take some action:
  - Read the issue.
  - If it's irrelevant now, please close the issue! That's the best thing to do.
  - If it's still relevant, add tags to the issue if there aren't any. Write a comment that you've seen it. Assign someone. Do something with it. Ask a question. In other words, don't just read it and let it go.

Thanks. Please help out if you have a few minutes. It would make me feel a lot better about the stability of our project if the number of issues were manageable.

Daniel

headache, so would just as soon close the issue.  But if
people feel strongly about it, it's trivial to code.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 4, 2016, at 5:22 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob!
>
> Well, computing power is ever to increase, so are laptops,to get more cpus soon

It's not really happening on notebooks due to power
consumption issues --- just on servers, where we're
getting more cores.

> ... And in modern computer clusters you can easily parallelize over 20 or more cores on a single machine. Only with threading you will make Stan scale to large problems.

What's funny is that everyone tells us a different thing is
the key to scaling.  There are really three candidates.  The
first two fall under making our current horse (er, algorithm)
run faster:

THREADING
Use multiple threads in a single process to make one chain go faster
   - could do this by parallelizing log-density/gradient calcs
   - parallelizing operations like matrix multiply/solve
   - running more exploration in parallel (faster adaptation, typical set
     finding, etc.) and allowing shared adaptation

GPUs
Again, we'd have to do the same kind of threading as above.

Then there's developing approximate algorithms, which is Andrew's
current hobby horse (I hope you appreciate today's equestrian theme).

Then there's building a horseless carriage (er, new algorithm),
where we have two candidates:

STOCHASTIC DATA STREAMING
Run subblocks of the data sequentially a la Robbins-Monro (e.g.,
Matt's stochastic VB)

DATA PARALLEL SOLUTIONS
Run data in parallel (e.g. Andrew's EP-like algorithms)

> My initial thought was to go poor mans approach, so instead of figuring out autmatically what can be thrown into threads, I would instead somehow augment the language. Notmsure yet how, maybe a parallel_for or whatever turns out to be smart after some research, a prototype and some discussions.

That's a very rich poor person!  But yes, it'd be great if we
could do any of the above things.  Word on the street is that GPUs
is where the action's at.  We've got gazillions (well tens of
thousands of them) on our cluster.

I'll reiterate that for the first two approaches, the trick is
going to be synchronizing the updates to the single autodiff stack.
Or figuring out how to also parallelize the reverse-mode step of
propagating derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: New Meeting Format
messages.body_plain:
With the increased number of participants at each dev meeting
we need to get a little more organized and unless there are
any objections I’m going to change things up on Tuesday.

In order to get important business out of the way before the
meeting becomes too tangential the meeting will now follow a
rigid progression:

1. Roundtable

Everyone very briefly reviews that they’ve been up to in the past
week (less than a minute, maybe more if they have been particularly productive).
This could be removed if there is enough support, but I think it’s
nice to touch base with everyone.

2. Unresolved Topics

These are topics carried over from the past meeting — they won’t
be applicable this week unless there are important issues that
were raised last week.  Let me know.

3. New Topics

These are topics of discussion that need to be addressed immediately
or before the next meeting, including questions about modeling or
development, well-posed requests for Stan features, or decisions that
have to be made.  New topics not immediately addressed at the meeting
will become “Unresolved topics” to be reviewed the following meeting.

4.  Open Discussion Topics

This is what our meetings typically devolve into right now, only hopefully
we can make it a bit more organized.  After all proposed discussion
topics have been covered we can open the meeting to other topics.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU:

If you hate this then let me know and we can try to find a compromise.

If there is anything that you want to have addressed next meeting
add it under “New Topics” at https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-Development-Meeting-Agenda.
If there are any any topics that you would like to discuss add then under
“Open Discussion Topics” at the same place.

This page is not meant for recording minutes or providing an archive
of meeting discussions — it’s just for organizing the meetings week
to week.

complex a;

in the Stan language would parse to

std::complex<stan::math::var> x;

is a compile-time error.

unnecessary, see https://www.discourse.org/about/ ("Wiki posts").

features. Since everything in a discussion thread is dated, it's very
easy to see whether or not something is out of date.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Adding StataStan unstable distribution page to github
messages.body_plain:
Hi, sorry for the delay in getting back to this topic. There is a command in Stata to install from a company-approved database of commands which is run by Kit Baum at Boston College, so to get StataStan, our users would most likely type:

ssc install windowsmonitor
ssc install stan

but there is also a command:

net install statastan, from("http://mc-stan.org/statastan")

which would fetch all the commands* it finds wrapped up by links in a .pkg file at the location. William Buchanan suggested this as a way of obtaining StataStan directly from GitHub and I thought it could provide a neat way to get the latest version, kind of like the stable release is through SSC and the unstable release is through github.io <http://github.io>

Both of these work with the current arrangement! But the unstable one needs some work. Sorry about the sparkly blue comic sans. I had no idea it would look so awful! All of this github pages stuff is new for me, and the last week or two have been too hectic to get to grips with it. So if anyone wants to step in and tweak the contents of gh-pages (equivalently http://mc-stan.org/statastan), feel free. Thanks to those who sent me stuff to read on this topic. It's in my inbox.

* - this is a pain. Stata use the term 'program' for what R users would call a function (but in part that's because Stata is, insofar as it is a language, not functional). But I think that's ambiguous, so I prefer to call it a command because that's what the user sees. Several commands can form a package through 'net install', but not through 'ssc install'. Once inside Stata, there are no packages, only commands. Urgh.

messages.subject: Stale Tests
messages.body_plain:
There are a huge number of “unit” tests which really just test
regression behavior.  These are particularly annoying because
there is absolutely no information about how the test content
was generated so that it can be updated when the code
necessitates it.  This kind of test makes development a
pain in the ass, and at the very least any such stale file
needs to also include how it was generated.

Examples include

stan-dev/cmdstan/src/test/interface/matrix_output.csv

There are also the files in

stan-dev/stan/src/test/unit/io/test_csv_files

These are particularly frustrating as they depend on CmdStan
which introduces a circular dependency in the repositories.  At
the same time, because they depend on static (usually static)
files they’ll pass even when there are inconsistencies.

Dan introduced all of these, so I think it’s fair that he provide
the code necessary to reproduce them.

> I think it came down to his not understanding and/or trusting
> ADVI (Andrew's comments are always subtly hedged, so I'm
> sure I'm doing him and ADVI a disservice trying to summarize).

1) The two algorithms answer two different questions.

ADVI tries to estimate _all_ marginal _means_.

MML tries to estimate _any_ marginal expectation with
respect to _a few chosen parameters_ (typically hyperparameters
in a hierarchical model).

2) Consequently the two algorithms lives on different points
of the speed/accuracy frontier.  Which is better for a given
application depends on the details of that application, which
means we’re entering into “expert-level knowledge needed”
territory.

Michael has it right. MML only concerns the marginal max of “high-level params” in that equation you write.

To do this, we do gradient descent. Gradient descent requires gradients of the marginal posterior density. This is hard because it’s a gradient of an expectation. Thus there’s an “E-step” in dealing with that expectation.

I think your confusion is about the relationship between EM and MM. You can view EM-type procedures as doing an “MM”, where computing expectations corresponds to maximizing something (for example, variational EM is an approximate “MM”).

Dustin

Remember that everything in statistics (really everything in measure theory)
is expectations.  Modes are only useful as a means to approximate
expectations, for example by approximating a target distribution with
a delta function at the mode,

\int dx p(x) f(x) \approx \int dx \delta_{x*} (x) f(x) = f(x*)

where

x* = argmax p(x).

Of course this isn’t parameterization invariant and is an atrocious estimator
in high dimensions unless there is an _insane_ amount of symmetry which
statistically translates to little or no corrections.

MML methods try to take a high dimensional problem and reduce it to a
lower dimensional one.  In particular, they partition the parameters x
into two sets, a low dimensional set y and a high dimensional set z,
x = (y, z).  If we could marginalize out the y analytically then we could
find the mode of p(y) which might be a useful approximation to some
expectations.  In practice we can’t do that, but we can approximate it,
which is what MML methods do.

The key computational step in MML methods is estimating the
conditional p(z | y) and then estimating

p(y) = \int dz p(z | y) p(y).

The conditional and the expectation are typically done with Gaussian
approximations.  The importance sampling step in GMO just tries to
correct these approximations to get more accurate estimates of the
marginal density.

messages.subject: GMO and MML
messages.body_plain:
Hi I don’t know if this will help, but . . .

1.  MML vs GMO

MML is a goal.  GMO is an algorithm.

MML is marginal maximum likelihood (more generally, marginal maximum penalized likelihood).  GMO is gradient-based marginal optimization, an algorithm (or class of algorithms) for reaching the MML solution using a particular approach to computing a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood function.  The GMO algorithm is similar to the ADVI algorithm in that it approximates the gradient directly, in contrast to the usual MML algorithms with approximate the marginal lilkelihood and then go from there.  It turns out it can make sense to go for the gradient directly, as we can then make use of the path sampling identity.

MML is to GMO as VB is to ADVI.

2.  Averaging and optimization in GMO

Conditional on the hyperparameters, GMO computes a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood.  This is the gradient of an integral, thus an integral of a gradient, thus it’s an integral.  But the way we simulation-estimate this integral is to start with a conditional mode-based approximation.  That’s why I say that GMO has an external optiimzation routine and an internal optimization routine. Really, it has an internal numerical integration routine, but it operates by first performing a conditional optimization.  It would be possible to run GMO without doing an internal optimzation; for example, the internal integral could be estimated using Nuts.  I’ve just been assuming that the mode-based approximation will be faster.

So, the internal integration is a necessary part of GMO.  The internal optimzation is not necessary, but it’s how we’ve been doing things.  The internal optimization is only there as a way to set up the internal integration.

GMO maximizes the marginal likelihood p(y | phi) to get phi^*. As you said, this is the problem of MML; everything else is an extension off that point estimate.

re:covariance. It’s an extension. As Bayesians, we view phi^* as a point mass approximation to the marginal posterior density p(phi | y). A cheap way to get uncertainty is to estimate the covariance of p(phi | y) using the inverse Hessian evaluated at phi^*. We can use this with phi^* to assume a normal approximation to p(phi | y), with mean phi^* and covariance H^{-1}(phi^*). This is like how in lm, it outputs both regression coefficients and their standard errors. Note: this still marginalizes over alpha.

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 8, 2016, at 10:07 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>

>> On Mar 8, 2016, at 9:49 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> 2.  Averaging and optimization in GMO
>>
>> Conditional on the hyperparameters, GMO computes a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood.  This is the gradient of an integral, thus an integral of a gradient, thus it’s an integral.  But the way we simulation-estimate this integral is to start with a conditional mode-based approximation.  That’s why I say that GMO has an external optiimzation routine and an internal optimization routine. Really, it has an internal numerical integration routine, but it operates by first performing a conditional optimization.  It would be possible to run GMO without doing an internal optimzation; for example, the internal integral could be estimated using Nuts.  I’ve just been assuming that the mode-based approximation will be faster.
>>
>> So, the internal integration is a necessary part of GMO.  The internal optimzation is not necessary, but it’s how we’ve been doing things.  The internal optimization is only there as a way to set up the internal integration.
>
> I also got that part of the algorithm, at least at a high
> level, by analogy to ADVI, which Alp wrote in language I
> could follow.
>
> But I thought GMO went even further in taking the MML + alpha* thing
> point estimate (phi*, alpha*) and created a multivariate normal
> approximation of the unconstrained posterior with mean (phi*, alpha*)
> and covariance given by the inverse Hessian at (phi*, alpha*).
>
> Then you take a bunch of draws from that multivariate normal and
> importance weight them, then transform back to the constrained space.
> Now if I take the importance-weighted average of the constrained draws,
> I'm not guaranteed to get (phi*, alpha*) as the posterior mean.
>
> So that'd be a rather different algorithm than MML.  But
> ADVI really is just an algorithm for computing a particular
> variational approximation and otherwise, the solution is the
> usual variational approximation.

At each “external” step (that is, guess of phi), GMO approximates the gradient of the integral p(phi,alpha|y) d alpha.  My particular idea of a GMO algorithm (so, I guess we could call this “GMO,” or at least the first recorded flavor of GMO) indeed first computed alpha*, then the normal approximation, then simulations, importance weighting, etc.  Don’t worry about constrained space for now; I’m assuming we’re entirely working in the unconstrained space.  The algoithm as written, with importnace sampling, gives a simulation-consistent estimate of the gradient of the integral.  So it really is a simulation-based approach to getting MML.  In practice, of course we don’t have infinitely many simulation draws so it’s only an approximation to MML, but that’s the same as ADVI and any other simulation-based integration.

messages.body_plain:
There’s a technical snippet that’s worth noting (to Andrew):

If we apply the path sampling identity to take the gradient of the marginal density (not the log marginal density), then there is no longer a ratio of expectations but one expectation. Importance sampling the one expectation gives us a simulation-consistent and also unbiased estimate of that gradient; therefore we can say it performs exact MML. Importance sampling a ratio of expectations as we currently do leads to a biased but simulation-consistent estimate (Appendix E in the write-up has the math). In practice, there’s no reason to do this over the ratio of expectations because optimizing on the original scale is more numerically unstable than optimizing on the log scale. But it’s nice to know that this variant exists.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GMO and MML
messages.body_plain:
> And is what people call "empirical Bayes" just
> full Bayes for p(alpha | phi*, y)?

Following Andrew’s point, I don’t know a good name for this. Another phrase thrown around is "Bayesian inference with data-dependent priors”. It is shorthand for "Bayesian inference with priors whose hyperparameters are point-estimated from the data”, which is what Bob wrote above in the case phi are prior hyperparameters. The general notion of “data-dependent priors” is also technically true for full Bayes, since the full posterior p(alpha, phi | y) has “data-dependent priors”. So I don’t know what to call it (if we should even call it something).

> P.S.  Dustin --- I'm putting this in Bayesian terms
> and avoiding max likelihood and std errors on purpose

Cool, we’re on the same page.

The first approach, using parenthesis, didn't work. The compiler returned the same error message, namely it complained about there being more than 10 expressions. I'm guessing the parenthesis are being ignored.

Here's my attempt at the second solution you proposed: I created a new expression rule, AdditionalArguments_r:

    stan::lang::expression AdditionalArguments_r;
    AdditionalArguments_r
      %= expression_g(_r1); // ss (data only)
       > lit(',')

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GMO and MML
messages.body_plain:
I still don't quite understand what GMO computes (specifically
how you get alpha*).

At least with HMC and NUTS I knew the goal was to draw a sample
from the posterior!

It's traditional in computer science to define the function
being computed before introducing an algorithm to compute it.
Working backwards to the function from the algorithm can be painful,
especially for those of us who don't know what MML or lme4 was doing.

- Bob

>>>>>
>>>>> 2.  Averaging and optimization in GMO
>>>>>
>>>>> Conditional on the hyperparameters, GMO computes a simulation-based estimate of the gradient of the marginal likelihood.  This is the gradient of an integral, thus an integral of a gradient, thus it’s an integral.  But the way we simulation-estimate this integral is to start with a conditional mode-based approximation.  That’s why I say that GMO has an external optiimzation routine and an internal optimization routine. Really, it has an internal numerical integration routine, but it operates by first performing a conditional optimization.  It would be possible to run GMO without doing an internal optimzation; for example, the internal integral could be estimated using Nuts.  I’ve just been assuming that the mode-based approximation will be faster.
>>>>>
>>>>> So, the internal integration is a necessary part of GMO.  The internal optimzation is not necessary, but it’s how we’ve been doing things.  The internal optimization is only there as a way to set up the internal integration.
>>>>
>>>> I also got that part of the algorithm, at least at a high
>>>> level, by analogy to ADVI, which Alp wrote in language I
>>>> could follow.
>>>>
>>>> But I thought GMO went even further in taking the MML + alpha* thing
>>>> point estimate (phi*, alpha*) and created a multivariate normal
>>>> approximation of the unconstrained posterior with mean (phi*, alpha*)
>>>> and covariance given by the inverse Hessian at (phi*, alpha*).
>>>>
>>>> Then you take a bunch of draws from that multivariate normal and
>>>> importance weight them, then transform back to the constrained space.
>>>> Now if I take the importance-weighted average of the constrained draws,
>>>> I'm not guaranteed to get (phi*, alpha*) as the posterior mean.
>>>>
>>>> So that'd be a rather different algorithm than MML.  But
>>>> ADVI really is just an algorithm for computing a particular
>>>> variational approximation and otherwise, the solution is the
>>>> usual variational approximation.
>>>
>>> At each “external” step (that is, guess of phi), GMO approximates the gradient of the integral p(phi,alpha|y) d alpha.  My particular idea of a GMO algorithm (so, I guess we could call this “GMO,” or at least the first recorded flavor of GMO) indeed first computed alpha*, then the normal approximation, then simulations, importance weighting, etc.  Don’t worry about constrained space for now; I’m assuming we’re entirely working in the unconstrained space.  The algoithm as written, with importnace sampling, gives a simulation-consistent estimate of the gradient of the integral.  So it really is a simulation-based approach to getting MML.  In practice, of course we don’t have infinitely many simulation draws so it’s only an approximation to MML, but that’s the same as ADVI and any other simulation-based integration.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GMO and MML
messages.body_plain:
With HMC and NUTS I knew the goal was to draw a sample from the posterior.

With GMO the goal is to compute the phi that maximizes p(phi | y) = int p(phi, alpha | y) d alpha.

There are also variants of GMO that compute some approximation.  But basic GMO aims for that argmax.

Knowing about lme4 is important if we’re interested in efficiency improvements for GMO.  But you don’t need to know about lme4 to understand GMO.

A

messages.subject: treedepth vs n_leapfrog
messages.body_plain:
Generically treedepth reports the size of the NUTS tree accepted
at each iteration but there is some ambiguity in what the number
of leapfrog steps should be.  There are three options

1) 2^{treedepth} = number of states that could have been sampled
    in the valid NUTS proposal.

2) 2^{treedepth} - 1 = number of new states that could have been
    sampled in the valid NUTS proposal.

3) Number of gradient evaluations.  This would also count the leapfrog
    steps in any subtrees that are rejected in each NUTS proposal.

Does anyone have any strong feelings one way or another?

For every real argument to a *function* in Stan, it
can either be a constant (data, transformed data, local
constant expression) or a parameter (parameter, transformed
parameter, local function of parameter).

The apparent exception is integrate_ode, but that's not
actually a function --- it's its own special syntax.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob!

Thanks for this summary, very informative. And sorry for sounding like threading would be the only thing to make Stan scale. This is certainly something which gave me in my past always very good performance and I think, given that Stan is typically used for hierarchical models, a parallel_for can help a lot in many typical models written in Stan.

Moreover, we have a cluster with hundreds of CPUs such that getting Stan running on those in parallel would be a reall jump forward. Of course, GPU approaches may even be better... that's well possible.

BTW, using the compiler extension openMP could also be an alternative for a platform independent way of threading for loops... From my experience openMP is very easy to use and openMP 3.0 is supported by all the compilers we care about (as I can tell on a quick look). Let's see, maybe this is worth a try.

Sebastian

I am not sure what might cause the limit. My guess is that one of the functions used in boost is overloaded to have between 0 and 10 arguments. This is the case for the ADD function used in function_signatures.h, which can have up to 7 arguments (for potentially interested viewers, the way around this limit is to use a vector of arguments, which only counts as one argument. It seems we are trying to do the same here, with the grammar rule being equivalent to a vector.)

The compiler does not explicitly state there is a 10 arguments limit. The error message is :

stan/lib/stan_math/lib/boost_1.58.0/boost/fusion/container/vector/convert.hpp:25:30: error:
      implicit instantiation of undefined template
      'boost::fusion::detail::barrier::as_vector<13>'

            typedef typename gen::
                             ^

where I have tried to create a function with 13 arguments. Note the as_vector<13> becomes as_vector<n> if I use n arguments. When n <= 10, this error no longer appears. This led me to think there was a 10 arguments limit.

The full error message is pasted at the end of this post.

I'll create an additional argument object (with 4 arguments), but I am unsure if this approach will work, given using  integrate_ode_cvode_r in lieu of expression_g(_r1) did not work. -- there is of course only one way to find out!

So, I hacked that together over a weekend years ago and it's terrible. Full on embarrassing that I did that type of terrible.

Can we redesign it so it's maintainable, robust, and isn't a tangled mess? Bob, I would feel much better if you were involved with design.

We don't need it in Stan anymore since the writer refactor happened and we can access output directly. We need to update tests so they don't depend on flat files within Stan. This should make Mike's work a lot easier to accomplish. (I think?)

Any takers?

Daniel

P.S. Krzysztof, if you wanted to deal with this one, it would help a lot. I'll keep thinking of other infrastructure places where we could use help.

Sure, I love this kind of thing.  I see two issues for a general design.

1.  Is it streaming or does it read the whole CSV file into
memory?  That is, do we need something like a row callback
or a data structure representing the whole matrix of entries, or
both?

2.  How do we deal with types?  Each column should have a type
such as integer, string, or double (other types?).

- Bob

Everything is read in as a string (if a name) or a double (if a value)

some Stan output file type so that we have a single output file
but all of the info separated.

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 14, 2016, at 2:03 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>>
>> 1.  Is it streaming or does it read the whole CSV file into
>> memory?  That is, do we need something like a row callback
>> or a data structure representing the whole matrix of entries, or
>> both?
>
> Reads everything in line by line, storing samples in an Eigen matrix.

As long as they're not too big, this will work.

All of our output summaries are by column (I think), so this would
be good for numerical locality.

>> 2.  How do we deal with types?  Each column should have a type
>> such as integer, string, or double (other types?).
>
> Everything is read in as a string (if a name) or a double (if a value)
> and then cast internally if necessary.

Then we'd need to know which is which before parsing.  Whereas
if we parse everything as a string, we can convert on reading.  But
it'll take more storage, so I'd rather predeclare if we have to store
everything as a data structure.  But then I'd suggest we need to do
it by column, because the types won't all be the same to store
in an Eigen matrix.

>
> Honestly I could be talked into splitting the output files into a
>
> model.meta (config + adaptation)
> model.warmup.csv (warmup iterations)
> mode.warmup.diag.csv (warmup iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
> model.samples.csv (sampling iterations)
> mode.samples.diag.csv (sampling iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
>
> so that we could easily stream all of the output statistic calculations.

I would very very strongly prefer that.  Then there's going to
be duplication for multiple chains, so it will be a pain to organize.
The easiest thing to do would be to assign a directory for a run.

We don't manage multiple chains from within CmdStan, but maybe
we should?  I think the x-platform multi-process issues are the killer.

> I would kill to have a generic way of stuffing all of those files into
> some Stan output file type so that we have a single output file
> but all of the info separated.

All else being equal, I'd prefer a generic format, like zip or gzipped tar,
so people can pull it out with usual desktop/unix tools.

Or we could do the whole thing with protocol buffers or something
like that, which require a bit more than desktop tools to unpack,
but could be much more concise if we work out the streaming details.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks --- that makes it clearer where the issue
is --- boost::fusion is the wrapper that converts
sequences into generic lists for template programming
and I'm pretty sure your diagnosis is spot on.

Either way, it's easy to work around with new intermediate
rules.

- Bob

This is the case for the ADD function used in function_signatures.h, which can have up to 7 arguments (for potentially interested viewers, the way around this limit is to use a vector of arguments, which only counts as one argument. messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Mar 14, 2016 at 2:16 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Mar 14, 2016, at 2:03 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >>
> >> 1.  Is it streaming or does it read the whole CSV file into
> >> memory?  That is, do we need something like a row callback
> >> or a data structure representing the whole matrix of entries, or
> >> both?
> >
> > Reads everything in line by line, storing samples in an Eigen matrix.
>
> As long as they're not too big, this will work.
>
> All of our output summaries are by column (I think), so this would
> be good for numerical locality.

Just to be clear, that's our current behavior. We read everything into memory. There's no requirement that we need to do that.

It's definitely easier to reason about things when everything is in memory. If you think we can stream it and it'll be ok, we can do that instead.

>
> >> 2.  How do we deal with types?  Each column should have a type
> >> such as integer, string, or double (other types?).
> >
> > Everything is read in as a string (if a name) or a double (if a value)
> > and then cast internally if necessary.
>
> Then we'd need to know which is which before parsing.  Whereas
> if we parse everything as a string, we can convert on reading.  But
> it'll take more storage, so I'd rather predeclare if we have to store
> everything as a data structure.  But then I'd suggest we need to do
> it by column, because the types won't all be the same to store
> in an Eigen matrix.

Within the non-commented lines, only the header contains strings. Everything else is numeric: either integer or floating point. Right now, we promote everything.

> >
> > Honestly I could be talked into splitting the output files into a
> >
> > model.meta (config + adaptation)
> > model.warmup.csv (warmup iterations)
> > mode.warmup.diag.csv (warmup iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
> > model.samples.csv (sampling iterations)
> > mode.samples.diag.csv (sampling iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
> >
> > so that we could easily stream all of the output statistic calculations.
>
> I would very very strongly prefer that.  Then there's going to
> be duplication for multiple chains, so it will be a pain to organize.
> The easiest thing to do would be to assign a directory for a run.
>
> We don't manage multiple chains from within CmdStan, but maybe
> we should?  I think the x-platform multi-process issues are the killer.

We could proc it, I think. I don't think we can reasonably multi-thread.

>
> > I would kill to have a generic way of stuffing all of those files into
> > some Stan output file type so that we have a single output file
> > but all of the info separated.
>
> All else being equal, I'd prefer a generic format, like zip or gzipped tar,
> so people can pull it out with usual desktop/unix tools.
>
> Or we could do the whole thing with protocol buffers or something
> like that, which require a bit more than desktop tools to unpack,
> but could be much more concise if we work out the streaming details.

I don't know how many people actually look at the csvs by hand. Here's what I think the normal workflow is.

1. Write foo.stan; compile foo, run foo, output into ___
2a. From CmdStan: ./bin/stansummary ___
2b. From RStan: fit <- read_stan_csv(___)

As long as we are able to maintain that workflow, I think we can change it around. Perhaps we no longer call it "read_stan_csv()." Or perhaps we write a CmdStan utility that outputs just the csv, but I think that's not so ideal.

> but all of the info separated.

So there's a protobuf-based writer that allows this sort of thing (mixing all the info in identifiable form into  a single broadly-readable file) on a separate repository at the moment:
https://github.com/sakrejda/protostan/blob/develop/src/protostan/interface_callbacks/writer/binary_proto_stream_writer.hpp

Note that a) I'm not claiming that this is better than a zipped directory for broad use/portability; and b) I'm  not saying the _design_ is right, but I have the mechanics of using protobuf for this down.  It would be pretty straightforward to do a similar format and then allow the user to run a reader over it to pull out specific pieces into .csv for command line usage or some sort of Eigen-compatible mmapable format.

On Monday, March 14, 2016 at 4:11:12 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> As a counter, I read the CSVs while the chains are running
> to monitor progress in hard models.  It’s very helpful for
> debugging.  The CmdStan UX should be much more than
> a crutch for RStan.

I do this too and I don't see how this would get in the way of rstan/pystan.

>
>
>
>
>
> On Mar 14, 2016, at 6:28 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
>
>
>
>
> On Mon, Mar 14, 2016 at 2:16 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Mar 14, 2016, at 2:03 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >>
> >> 1.  Is it streaming or does it read the whole CSV file into
> >> memory?  That is, do we need something like a row callback
> >> or a data structure representing the whole matrix of entries, or
> >> both?
> >
> > Reads everything in line by line, storing samples in an Eigen matrix.
>
> As long as they're not too big, this will work.
>
> All of our output summaries are by column (I think), so this would
> be good for numerical locality.
>
>
>
>
> Just to be clear, that's our current behavior. We read everything into memory. There's no requirement that we need to do that.
>
>
> It's definitely easier to reason about things when everything is in memory. If you think we can stream it and it'll be ok, we can do that instead.
>
>
>
>
> >> 2.  How do we deal with types?  Each column should have a type
> >> such as integer, string, or double (other types?).
> >
> > Everything is read in as a string (if a name) or a double (if a value)
> > and then cast internally if necessary.
>
> Then we'd need to know which is which before parsing.  Whereas
> if we parse everything as a string, we can convert on reading.  But
> it'll take more storage, so I'd rather predeclare if we have to store
> everything as a data structure.  But then I'd suggest we need to do
> it by column, because the types won't all be the same to store
> in an Eigen matrix.
>
>
>
> Within the non-commented lines, only the header contains strings. Everything else is numeric: either integer or floating point. Right now, we promote everything.
>
>  >
> > Honestly I could be talked into splitting the output files into a
> >
> > model.meta (config + adaptation)
> > model.warmup.csv (warmup iterations)
> > mode.warmup.diag.csv (warmup iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
> > model.samples.csv (sampling iterations)
> > mode.samples.diag.csv (sampling iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
> >
> > so that we could easily stream all of the output statistic calculations.
>
> I would very very strongly prefer that.  Then there's going to
> be duplication for multiple chains, so it will be a pain to organize.
> The easiest thing to do would be to assign a directory for a run.
>
> We don't manage multiple chains from within CmdStan, but maybe
> we should?  I think the x-platform multi-process issues are the killer.
>
>
>
> We could proc it, I think. I don't think we can reasonably multi-thread.
>
>
>
> > I would kill to have a generic way of stuffing all of those files into
> > some Stan output file type so that we have a single output file
> > but all of the info separated.
>
> All else being equal, I'd prefer a generic format, like zip or gzipped tar,
> so people can pull it out with usual desktop/unix tools.
>
> Or we could do the whole thing with protocol buffers or something
> like that, which require a bit more than desktop tools to unpack,
> but could be much more concise if we work out the streaming details.
>
>
> I don't know how many people actually look at the csvs by hand. Here's what I think the normal workflow is.
>
>
> 1. Write foo.stan; compile foo, run foo, output into ___
>
> 2a. From CmdStan: ./bin/stansummary ___
>
> 2b. From RStan: fit <- read_stan_csv(___)
>
>
> As long as we are able to maintain that workflow, I think we can change it around. Perhaps we no longer call it "read_stan_csv()." Or perhaps we write a CmdStan utility that outputs just the csv, but I think that's not so ideal.
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [math] convert arguments to MatrixBase<T> (#62)
messages.body_plain:
On Sun, Mar 13, 2016 at 12:38:44PM -0700, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>    To summarize, the heart of the problem with correctness
>    and template expressions here is:
>    1. Eigen returns fundamentally different kinds of template
>    expressions for arithmetic operations and blocking operations
>    2. MatrixBase deals with one and Ref deals with the other; Ref
>    is nice and general, but type inference won't work through it.
>    The only solution I see is to either
>    A. rewrite the library to accept both inputs (lots of code)
>    B. rewrite the library to accept just MatrixBase and
>    make sure we never return block() operations (trades one
>    kind of efficiency for the other)
>    So I'm not clear on what you think we should do.
>    There are at least three other ways we can speed up basic
>    matrix math:
>    * better memory locality blocking algorithms for the matrix
>    autodiff functions (potential order of magnitude speedup here)
>    * CPU parallelism with multithreading in both matrix libs
>    and in ODE solvers and in our density calculations
>    * GPU callouts from matrix ops (potential order of magnitude or
>    more speedup here, conditioned on doing the above first so
>    everything's not memory bound)

Any solution here seems so complicated that I give up. I suspect C++
(even C++17) just isn't up to the task.

Has anybody spent some time looking closely at Rust,
https://www.rust-lang.org/ ?

--
Joshua N. Pritikin
Department of Psychology
University of Virginia
485 McCormick Rd, Gilmer Hall Room 102
Charlottesville, VA 22904
http://people.virginia.edu/~jnp3bc

messages.subject: Re: Where to put vectorize files
messages.body_plain:
[moved to stan-dev]

1.  All mail like this should go to stan-dev if at all possible,
rather than just to individuals.

2.  All discussion clarifying the design should go in the
appropriate issue in the tracker.

To answer your questions, implicit and explicit:

1.  The function definitions so should go here:

```
stan/math/prim/mat/fun/<function-name>.hpp
```

2.  For functions already partly vectorized, you need
to remove the original vectorized definitions (just get
rid of them and their associated tests).

3.  The function signatures class is going to need a utility
method to declare these, presumably something like
``add_unary_vectorized("exp") and so on.

This should declare all the basic vectorizations and
perhaps up to 4 deep for arrays of all types.

4.  You're going to need to write (or have me write)
    a.  a new intro section to the functions guide in the manual,
        with some new syntax for this vectorization, and
    b.  update the doc for each of the added functions

- Bob

Hi!

upgrading boost is already long in the issue tracker. Any obvious reason no update has been made yet?

What are the requirements for acceptance when we upgrade boost? I mean, in this case to my knowledge things still work for Stan, but you end up getting some warning messages from the compiler due to some deprecated stuff. So is it required to address those deprecated messages right away when taking care of the upgrade. Or can we push these secondary issues into further issues?

The boost odeint solver has gotten a very important upgrade (implementation of max_num_step functionality) which I would like to enable ASAP.

Sebastian

> On Mar 16, 2016, at 6:24 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

So is it required to address those deprecated messages right away when taking care of the upgrade. Or can we push these secondary issues into further issues?

We move forward when the bh package in R (boost headers) move forward. For every interface other than R, we distribute boost.

It's a matter of practical integration issues. If we move forward with the boost version before bh, then it's very possible some part of Stan will be incompatible with one of our major interfaces.

This is the same reason we haven't gone to c++11.

On Tuesday, March 15, 2016 at 3:31:46 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks for creating the Wiki.

Sure, I was hoping we could get input on the desirable characteristics
now and rank them rather than doing design by feature creep later.

> I agree that there's a large benefit from using an
> easily human/machine-readable format like CSV.  If
> we had something like a protocol buffer output or
> JSON file, we'd probably want utilities that could read
> it and produce the relevant CSV files,

Yep, producing .csv files is not something we can avoid.

> but that's a lot
> of extra work (with the benefit of probably much smaller
> and much faster output, not that output in sampling is really our
> bottleneck).

It's not necessarily a lot of extra work: we have to do the
design work anyway and as long as we're willing to rely on one
of the serialization libraries the design issues are more about
creating a schema for Stan data rather than designing a
serialization format.

The other benefit of a binary-first strategy is that we have
the potential for round-tripping output state (samples and, say,
mass matrix) to inits which is
another desirable feature.

Krzysztof

> - Bob

messages.subject: output format
messages.body_plain:
The csv_reader discussion started an output format discussion.  If you have options that should be considered, or want to add to the discussion notes so far, they are here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Output-format

I'm ok with doing exploration around suggested libraries but (as you'll see from the JSONlines entry) if I can't think of positives for an option, I won't try very hard.  I think we can have this discussion now and settle on a overall strategy soon.  I'm on board for implementing something (reasonable in scope) and, as suggested by Daniel, I'm hoping Bob can keep the design to something practical.

It would be great to make this a short-term project so if you have opinions pile on now... (here or at the Wiki page if it's more concrete).  Having a good set format and tools to make it compatible with multiple interfaces would make the whole Stan-for-everything strategy a lot easier on interface maintainers.

Krzysztof

We don't do that in the C++.  We promote ints to doubles, but *not*
vice-versa.   It's a disaster for both speed and error handling.

R just works the way R works, and it seemed to much of people
to ask them to explicitly make 1 an integer because R just
straight-up assumes it's a double if not otherwise informed.
Our own data parsing does the opposite.

I blame the interfaces.  For the command line, the interface is the
command line itself, which is a string.  So we pretty much have to

We can try to accomodate other interfaces other than CmdStan
with a format that includes the chain ID.  I don't think it's

messages.subject: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
One of the common problems that we keep running into is that
everyone has different, and usually incomplete, understandings
of probability.  Of course probability theory is relatively abstract
and we’re not going to be able to teach it to those without
reasonable math backgrounds: in that case the approaches
of McElreath and Kruschke are probably best.  What doesn’t
exist in the literature is an introductory treatment of probability
theory and inference that goes into all of the technical details
for those who do have a reasonable math background.  I’m
talking about concepts like concentration of measure, the
difference between probability, probability mass functions,
and probability density function.

Anyways, I think we’re going to need a treatment like that
in the Stan manual going forward, and this is my best
attempt at an initial draft, https://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro/blob/master/stan_intro.pdf.
Conditioned on a familiarity with calculus everything should,
hopefully, be self-contained and well-defined.

The inference section is still a little bit in flux, but I’m really
happy about the general organization of the probability sections.
That said, I’m sure there are many topics that unclear or
too hastily introduced or could use more examples to build
intuition, so let me have it.  Either here on the list or via an
issue/PR.  Otherwise let me know what you think.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
I looked it as well and think it’s excellent. It organizes a lot of ideas that I wish were presented this way more often (e.g., I really like section 5’s presentation on MAP estimators as dirac point mass approximations, Laplace estimators as the previous+covariance, variational estimators as optimization given a divergence function).

That said, I can’t tell how feasible this is for a person just getting into probability, even assuming the person has all the necessary mathematical background. It all seems too abstract to get a good handle of these objects as a first exposure. Joe Blitzstein and Carl Morris have an ongoing book manuscript on probability theory for statistical sciences that caters to the applied realm very well; they have several organizational techniques that might be useful here.

I like the separation of estimators into deterministic and stochastic; I also took a similar route as I’m writing this Python package that does statistical inference, and the internals use two base classes which correspond to these two paradigms. I wanted to mention one caveat, which is that the distinction can be quite blurry and it could be important to be mindful of these complications. As some examples which I’m sure you’re familiar with: a MAP optimization procedure with constant learning rate can converge with the target distribution as the stationary distribution; stochastic approximation theory uses Monte Carlo estimators within the steps to reach a stationary point and is not deterministic; and the expressiveness of the approximating family can grow unboundedly to indeed include the posterior as one such member in the family.

Dustin

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
I'm about halfway through reading it pretty closely.
I think I get everything --- the math's at just the right level
for me now, and I like how it's finessing some of the more
complex definitions (a la Baez's awesome intro to manifolds).

What it needs is some more concrete examples (ones involving
trig are tough---if someone doesn't understand change of
variables, like I didn't, all those trig based examples are
complicated --- I needed to work through lognormal to "get
it").

It's all slightly unusual because rather than introducing
abstract sigma-algebras and random variables, everything's
baked into the space, so all the random variables are
projections (although the whole issue of random variables
is sidestepped).  This makes it easy to generate sample spaces
by construction, whereas the usual level of indirection could be
confusing.  I don't think I understood sample spaces until I
went through this construction myself.  This got a little confusing
in the mass function setting, because in general, I can have a
continuous sample space (like a dartboard) and discrete
outcomes (like which wedge it falls in), to produce a mass
function.  And I think what Michael's doing amounts to the same
thing in that there'd be three variables, x, y, and discrete
outcome, which are tightly coupled.  If I understood what Michael
was up to, that is.

- Bob

Hi, Bob. You are saying that it's at the right level for you now. Just noting that most, if not all y'all, are Ph.D's (or at least post-grads) in math or computer science. Many of the users, such as myself, will not have such a rigorous grounding in statistics. We'll probably have more than nothing (Masters, actuarial exams, self-taught/online courses, etc.)

While most of what I have read so far (and I have not finished it yet) is rather accessible to the educated layperson, I'd put in a request for a little more explanation of some of the more esoteric concepts. For example, I'm very happy that Michael takes the time to explain probability spaces (something with which most practitioners will have little experience) but would be very appreciative if a little more exposition was made about conditional probability and what exactly the auxiliary space is and how it interacts with the unconditional probability space.

I've noticed a few typos/grammar errors. Would you want an issue for those or a fork/pull request on the LaTeX file?

Thanks,

Avi

for people with good math skills (I took topology and a year of

the appendix to Anderson and Moore's book on Optimal Filtering.

consistently in a way very few other sources do.  But no examples,
so it's more of a good way to consolidate understanding than to
learn from.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
> What it needs is some more concrete examples (ones involving
> trig are tough---if someone doesn't understand change of
> variables, like I didn't, all those trig based examples are
> complicated --- I needed to work through lognormal to "get
> it”).

I’m happy to add more examples if people can suggest
useful ones, but I do have the warning about knowing
calculus specifically for the reason that things like
Jacobians and change of variables won’t make sense
without it.

> It's all slightly unusual because rather than introducing
> abstract sigma-algebras and random variables, everything's
> baked into the space, so all the random variables are
> projections (although the whole issue of random variables
> is sidestepped).  This makes it easy to generate sample spaces
> by construction, whereas the usual level of indirection could be
> confusing.

Typically the material is presented as an abstract probability
triplet (sample space, sigma algebra, and probability distribution)
that doesn’t have any meaningful sense of value.  Then random
variables map that system onto R or some R^{n} which does
have value, basically defining a “measurement” of the abstract
system.  Then you go through all of the rigamarole of pushing
the sigma algebra and probability distribution forward onto
the image of the random variable to give a new probability
system you can actually calculate with using calculus.  But
if you ignore all of the intermediate steps then all you’ve
done is changed representations (and maybe marginalized).

I never liked any of that as it’s never how things are done
operationally, hence my focus on equivalent sample spaces
as just being a representation degeneracy, which is ultimately
all it is.

> I don't think I understood sample spaces until I
> went through this construction myself.  This got a little confusing
> in the mass function setting, because in general, I can have a
> continuous sample space (like a dartboard) and discrete
> outcomes (like which wedge it falls in), to produce a mass
> function.  And I think what Michael's doing amounts to the same
> thing in that there'd be three variables, x, y, and discrete
> outcome, which are tightly coupled.  If I understood what Michael
> was up to, that is.

This is a slightly particular example — if you can partition a
sample space into sets then you can always construct a discrete
probabilistic system implicitly by the mass function with takes

p(x_{1}) = \mathbb{P} [ A_{1} ].

Kind of like a singular marginalization from a continuous space
into a discrete one.
