messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
As I noted in the original email, this is not meant as a gentle introduction
to people who want to learn about probability but don’t like math.  In fact,
I _really_ don’t like trying to teach probability without some mathematical
foundation, because all it leads to is paradoxes and confusion!

What always happens is that people try to introduce probability theory
with probability densities and then inevitably everyone gets confused
with what are probabilities and what are densities and intuiting probability
as density and then becoming frustrated.

Or you could stick to probabilities over discrete spaces, but then you
don’t get to do anything on continuous spaces, which means no Gaussians
and other members of the exponential family.

This introduction is meant as the minimal material needed to really understand
statistical computation so that there are no “gotchya!”s that will bite the reader
later when they try to apply any lessons to real problems.  Note that I went
to great effort to focus on concepts and relationships between concepts and
not on unhelpful calculation or proofs.

I am happy to add more examples and spend more time expositing on concepts
(suggestions, please!) At the same time, however, we have to be careful that
the reader doesn’t take the examples too seriously and lose some of the
necessary generality/abstraction.

Many of the users, such as myself, will not have such a rigorous grounding in statistics. We'll probably have more than nothing (Masters, actuarial exams, self-taught/online courses, etc.)
>
> While most of what I have read so far (and I have not finished it yet) is rather accessible to the educated layperson, I'd put in a request for a little more explanation of some of the more esoteric concepts. For example, I'm very happy that Michael takes the time to explain probability spaces (something with which most practitioners will have little experience) but would be very appreciative if a little more exposition was made about conditional probability and what exactly the auxiliary space is and how it interacts with the unconditional probability space.
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayes Factors via product spaces?
messages.body_plain:
You're always in one model or the other in Stan, too.
It's just that we marginalize out the mixture indicator
parameter.  That should just make computation more efficient.

The key to implementing anything in Stan is to understand
what density you want to fit.  If you can write the model
down in JAGS, that will determine the density you're fitting.
Then we should be able to code it in Stan directly.

- Bob

> On Mar 22, 2016, at 11:52 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Is there any update on this thus far?  I happened to stumble on this post from googling about a stan implementation of the product space method.
>
> Intuitively it seems like one could implement a similar concept in stan.
>
> The key in bugs/jags is that you're always in one model or another.
> When in model 1, you're estimating model 1 with some probability of switching to model 2, where model 2's "priors" are evaluated as the posterior of model 2 (previously estimated). The latter is *only* to make jumping easier. I don't think it's actually required for computing the BF in theory, it just helps with mixing.
>
> Could one do something analogous?
> In stan, one can pit two models against each other as a mixture; (p[1]likelihood[1] + p[2]likelihood[2])*priors.
> I tried this and of course it didn't seem to 'work'; I had an intercept-only model and a full model, and the probability of each was roughly .5 (no change from prior of ~logistic(0,1)).
> Or several chains would converge to suggest p[1] was much higher, although BayesFactor suggests the opposite (this seems highly dependent on initial values).
> I'm using the example from the BayesFactor package (below).
>
> Is it possible to conditionally set priors, or to 'weight' the priors themselves by the probability of each model?
>
>
> library(BayesFactor)
> library(rstan)
> data(attitude)
> ds <- attitude
> ds <- scale(ds)
> options(mc.cores=parallel::detectCores())
> rstan_options(auto_write=TRUE)
>
> bf.stan <- "
> data{
>     int N;
>     int J;
>     matrix[N,J] y;
> }
>
> parameters {
>     vector[6] beta;
>     real intercept[2];
>     real<lower=0> resid[2];
>     real p_logis;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>     simplex[2] p;
>
>     p[2] <- exp(p_logis)/(1 + exp(p_logis));
>     p[1] <- 1 - p[2];
> }
>
> model {
> real lp_k[2];
> real lp;
> vector[N] yhat[2];
>     beta ~ cauchy(0,1);
>     intercept ~ cauchy(0,1);
>     resid ~ cauchy(0,1);
>     p_logis ~ logistic(0,1);
>
>     for(n in 1:N){
>         yhat[1,n] <- intercept[1];
>         yhat[2,n] <- intercept[2] + y[n,2:7]*beta;
>     }
>     lp_k[1] <- log(p[1]) + normal_log(y'[1],yhat[1],rep_vector(resid[1],N));
>     lp_k[2] <- log(p[2]) + normal_log(y'[1],yhat[2],rep_vector(resid[2],N));
>     lp <- log_sum_exp(lp_k);
>     increment_log_prob(lp);
> }
> "
> stanOut <- stan(model_code=bf.stan,data=list(y=ds,N=30,J=7),iter=10000,chains=8)

>
>
>
>
>
> On Monday, November 3, 2014 at 5:00:19 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I was not able to definitively answer Martin Smira's question
> about whether it would be possible to implement the product-space
> approach to Bayes factor computations with HMC.
>
> This was developed by Carlin and Chib:
>
>   B.P. Carlin, S. Chib
>   Bayesian model choice via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
>   Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57 (1995), pp. 473–484
>
> There's also an overview in a (paywalled) psych journal that kicked
> off the discussion (Lee and Wagenmakers are two of the co-authors):
>
>   http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022249611000423
>
> And there's a discussion by Charles Geyer in the umbrella sampling chapter of
> the MCMC Handbook (not one of the free chapters, I'm afraid).
>
> The most explicit reference I saw for how a model like this can be
> coded is in a BUGS vol2 example:
>
>   http://www.medicine.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/joseph/courses/EPIB-682/pines.pdf
>
> We do not have that example working in Stan, nor could I get a version
> working.  From what I can tell, the product-space approach simulates a reversible
> jump MCMC method with Gibbs sampling and pseudo-priors, with some fiddly
> pre-tuning required to adjust the pseudo-priors.  But I'm afraid I don't even
> understand why it'd work in BUGS because the posterior just looks wrong (so there's
> probably something I'm not understanding --- like maybe they only take the parameter
> samples from one of the branches [which clearly won't work in Stan]).
>
> I had problems trying to conceptualize what the model would even look
> like in Stan and was wondering if anyone had any suggestions or an explanation
> of why it wouldn't be possible.
>
> - Bob
>

uses the language of random variables, like BDA.

messages.subject: include-what-you-use on Mac
messages.body_plain:
This is going to be most relevant to Bob. I'll throw this on a wiki page in a bit, but here's how to install and run on a Mac.

Installation
--------------------
Easy installation requires Homebrew.
Steps:
1. brew tap jasonmp85/iwyu
2. brew install iwyu

More details: https://github.com/jasonmp85/homebrew-iwyu

Running include-what-you-use on the parser
------------------------------------------------------------
Once iwyu has been installed:
    make -k test/test-models/stanc CC=iwyu &> iwyu.out

Inspect iwyu.out.

More info:
- "-k" flag continues running make in the presence of errors. iwyu always returns an error code, so omitting that will stop at the first compilation.
- "CC=iwyu" just replaces the compiler with iwyu. iwyu doesn't support the full set of compiler flags, so it'll put up warnings about some of our compiler flags.
- "&> iwyu.out" just grabs the output in both the stdout and stderr and puts it into iwyu.out.

I haven't figured out how to run this over our whole code base.

Daniel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] CmdStan's stan_csv_reader (which is in the Stan Library)
messages.body_plain:
I see two things that this is trying to do.

Specify what the output is supposed to be for Stan.
A very good thing to do.

Specify how the writers work at a low level to make
sure we can express all that output.

Make a concrete, cross-interface proposal for a serialized
form of all this data as multiple files per chain, multiple
chains per run.

Round-trip is definitely a desirable goal.  We can do it
in RStan pretty easily, but not in CmdStan (again, I have
no clue about PyStan).

- Bob

> On Mar 16, 2016, at 10:09 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, March 15, 2016 at 3:31:46 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Thanks for creating the Wiki.
>
> Sure, I was hoping we could get input on the desirable characteristics
> now and rank them rather than doing design by feature creep later.
>
>
>> I agree that there's a large benefit from using an
>> easily human/machine-readable format like CSV.  If
>> we had something like a protocol buffer output or
>> JSON file, we'd probably want utilities that could read
>> it and produce the relevant CSV files,
>
> Yep, producing .csv files is not something we can avoid.
>
>> but that's a lot
>> of extra work (with the benefit of probably much smaller
>> and much faster output, not that output in sampling is really our
>> bottleneck).
>
> It's not necessarily a lot of extra work: we have to do the
> design work anyway and as long as we're willing to rely on one
> of the serialization libraries the design issues are more about
> creating a schema for Stan data rather than designing a
> serialization format.
>
> The other benefit of a binary-first strategy is that we have
> the potential for round-tripping output state (samples and, say,
> mass matrix) to inits which is
> another desirable feature.
>
> Krzysztof
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Mar 15, 2016, at 11:42 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> On Tuesday, March 15, 2016 at 10:36:58 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>>> I would much prefer to keep at least the sample info
>>>> in CSV format as it makes it super easy to use with
>>>> other packages (in my case, graphics libraries).
>>>
>>> I made a quick summary of the things people have asked for so far:
>>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Output-format
>>>
>>> I'm willing to keep doing summaries as this discussion goes on and gets to a decision.
>>>
>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> On Mar 15, 2016, at 2:05 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> On 03/14, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
>>>> On Monday, March 14, 2016 at 2:03:12 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>>>
>>>> 1.  Is it streaming or does it read the whole CSV file into
>>>> memory?  That is, do we need something like a row callback
>>>> or a data structure representing the whole matrix of entries, or
>>>> both?
>>>>
>>>> Reads everything in line by line, storing samples in an Eigen matrix.
>>>>
>>>> 2.  How do we deal with types?  Each column should have a type
>>>> such as integer, string, or double (other types?).
>>>>
>>>> Everything is read in as a string (if a name) or a double (if a value)
>>>> and then cast internally if necessary.
>>>>
>>>> Honestly I could be talked into splitting the output files into a
>>>>
>>>> model.meta (config + adaptation)
>>>> model.warmup.csv (warmup iterations)
>>>> mode.warmup.diag.csv (warmup iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
>>>> model.samples.csv (sampling iterations)
>>>> mode.samples.diag.csv (sampling iterations but unconstrained and with gradients and momenta)
>>>>
>>>> so that we could easily stream all of the output statistic calculations.
>>>>
>>>> I would kill to have a generic way of stuffing all of those files into
>>>> some Stan output file type so that we have a single output file
>>>> but all of the info separated.
>>>>
>>>> So there's a protobuf-based writer that allows this sort of thing (mixing all the info in identifiable form into  a single broadly-readable file) on a separate repository at the moment:
>>>> https://github.com/sakrejda/protostan/blob/develop/src/protostan/interface_callbacks/writer/binary_proto_stream_writer.hpp
>>>>
>>>> Note that a) I'm not claiming that this is better than a zipped directory for broad use/portability; and b) I'm  not saying the _design_ is right, but I have the mechanics of using protobuf for this down.  It would be pretty straightforward to do a similar format and then allow the user to run a reader over it to pull out specific pieces into .csv for command line usage or some sort of Eigen-compatible mmapable format.
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> Another option would be to stream everything into file
>>>> ``model.jsonlines`` where each line was a valid JSON object, see
>>>> http://jsonlines.org/

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] unit vectors?
messages.body_plain:
I played with this issue a while back and have some notes that I'll try to dig up.  I've been meaning to finish and publish them, so maybe this will be an incentive.

Anyway, there is a way to do this which is legit.  It involves introducing an auxiliary variable which is the norm of the unconstrained vector and giving it a density.

To be concrete (if not formal):

Unconstrained space: x \in \R^K
Constrained space: d \in S^{K+1}, r \in \R^+  (i.e., r is strictly positive)

Transformations are then:

Unconstrained -> Constrained: d = x / ||x||, r = ||x||
Constrained -> Unconstrained: x = r*d

Where r is an auxiliary variable.  Now you have a standard, invertible transformation which you can treat using change of variables just like anything else.

To ensure the distribution on x is proper we assume the user defines a (proper) posterior on d but we need a proper distribution on r.  I believe what Ben had long ago proposed (and was probably what got implemented in Stan right now, I haven't checked) is to put a N(0,1) distribution on x, and this corresponds to something like a chi distribution on r with K DoFs.  Anyway, if you do this, then you get a well defined transformation and a proper distribution on the unconstrained space.

The practical issues are:
1) We need to incorporate the distribution on r implicitly and
2) We don't care about r and don't really want to have to keep track of it.

Issue 1 can be fixed by including the distribution over r along with the Jacobian correction.  Issue 2 is also pretty easy, since the distribution over d is invariant to r so we can discard the value of r when we transform to the constrained space and we can choose an arbitrary value for it (e.g., 1) when transform to the unconstrained space.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2
messages.subject_clean: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2
messages.body_plain:
The stan_lm function in rstanarm implements a linear model with regularizing priors driven by prior beliefs about the R^2. This has been confusing to many users and pretty much everyone except for Ben (who had the idea for this cool prior). In light of the confusion, I've written a rough draft of a paper about the prior and I would very much appreciate some feedback. The latest version is attached as a pdf. You can also find the pdf as well as the raw .tex file and R code for the graphics on GitHub in my R2prior repository <https://github.com/jgabry/R2prior>.

The paper is pretty short (9 pages or so) so it should be a quick read.

Thanks,

Jonah

messages.subject: cleaning up Stan output
messages.body_plain:
Currently Stan outputs an update every 10th of the run.  That’s 40 outputs in a typical 4-chain run.  40 lines of output makes it impossible to read the console.

Here’s my proposal:

1.  Just spit out two messages:  one after 10% of warmup iterations giving estimated total time, another after 10% of the sampling iterations with an updated estimated time, since they can be faster than warmup.

2.  Just print one pair of messages on the console, no matter how many chains are running.  Simplest would be to just wait until all 4 (or however many) chains have sent out their 10% messages, then print the latest of these onto the console.

3.  Also we should have a no-print option.  We could have multiple verbose settings, but I’d like a default that is something like my suggestion above, also a no-print option, also maybe an option that prints out more, that I dunno.

A

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, March 24, 2016 at 5:28:57 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks.  Got it.  The Wikipedia article was very clear (even though
> it didn't have any justification).  I think it's saying the same thing
> as Marcus, with the radius being the "auxiliary" variable that gets
> a unit normal distribution.

I think that is not what Marcus is saying. We only need the transformation from a unit_simplex to the unconstrained space for initial values. So, if someone gives a valid unit_simplex as an initial value, then just take r to be 1.0 and copy the unit_simplex into the "unconstrained" space. Then when the action starts, it will take the thing in the unconstrained space and divide by its Euclidean norm (which is 1.0) to create the unit_vector. Then it moves in the unconstrained space to something without a norm of 1.0 but it normalizes to form the unit vector.

We already have the unit_vector_constrain and unit_vector_free functions, but when it creates a model where a unit_vector is a parameter, it makes it too short by one element.

> And I take it that it means that the "Jacobian" is really just the normal
> and I don't need another Jacobian correction in there?

Right, the form of the Jacobian determinant is a product of standard normal kernels, which is implemented in log-form by unit_vector_constrain. Or equivalently, putting a standard normal prior on the unconstrained parameters implies a uniform prior on the unit_vector. It is a very similar principle to putting particular symmetric beta priors on canonical partial correlations implies a uniform prior on a correlation matrix.

Ben

> Jonah

messages.subject: Re: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
I really enjoyed reading the text, although I'm biased as I'm familiar
with the topic. I guess many of my master level students would have
difficulties but those same have have difficulties with BDA, too. I'll
give this to some of my more advanced students to read, too.  Overall
it's an excellent overview (or beginning of such overview) and answers
many FAQs in the Stan users list.

One specific comment. You write
"Consequently the small world is equivalent to a probability distribution over the measurements space conditioned on the small world,
...
This conditional probability distribution is also known as the likelihood."

p(d|theta) as a function of d is conditional probability distribution.

p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which
is not a probability distribution. Sometimes it's proportional to a
probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required
to make it possible to normalise the posterior.

I think it is important to make this distinction to have a different
name for p(d|theta) and L(d|theta), but also because the models are
often described as generative models using conditional probability
distributions (observation models), but in Stan we often also write
some terms of log likelihood directly (e.g. for models with
censoring). I think that the new notation is also making it more
explicit that we are making statements about parameters theta.

Aki

 Friday, March 18, 2016 at 1:47:10 AM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> One of the common problems that we keep running into is that
> everyone has different, and usually incomplete, understandings
> of probability.  Of course probability theory is relatively abstract
> and we’re not going to be able to teach it to those without
> reasonable math backgrounds: in that case the approaches
> of McElreath and Kruschke are probably best.  What doesn’t
> exist in the literature is an introductory treatment of probability
> theory and inference that goes into all of the technical details
> for those who do have a reasonable math background.  I’m
> talking about concepts like concentration of measure, the
> difference between probability, probability mass functions,
> and probability density function.
>
> Anyways, I think we’re going to need a treatment like that
> in the Stan manual going forward, and this is my best
> attempt at an initial draft, https://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro/blob/master/stan_intro.pdf.
> Conditioned on a familiarity with calculus everything should,
> hopefully, be self-contained and well-defined.
>
> The inference section is still a little bit in flux, but I’m really
> happy about the general organization of the probability sections.
> That said, I’m sure there are many topics that unclear or
> too hastily introduced or could use more examples to build
> intuition, so let me have it.  Either here on the list or via an
> issue/PR.  Otherwise let me know what you think.

messages.subject: model that compiles in CmdStan but not RStan
messages.subject_clean: model that compiles in CmdStan but not RStan
messages.body_plain:
I was about to try and fix

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1810

when I realized that it works just fine in CmdStan (though it does
find a signed vs. unsigned comparison issue in g++ 4.7).

I don't want to just move this issue over to RStan without
checking whether it's caused by something in Stan or Stan Math.

I verified the issue is *not* because of Eigen 3.2.8;  it still
compiles in CmdStan with Eigen 3.2.8 plugged in.  And CmdStan works
fine with both g++4.7 and clang++ (whatever the recent flavor is
in Xcode).

The compile error arises from an instantiation of the generated
model class in rstan/stan_fit.hpp and it looks like
SEXPREC* is getting pasted in and interpreted as a numerical
type and Eigen can't figure out how to assign to it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2
messages.subject_clean: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2
messages.body_plain:
The draft made R^2 prior more clear for me. Here are few quick comments

- I just remembered that one of our papers http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0029115
has a discussion on prior beliefs about the R^2 using similar (but different) approach as the approach by Guan and Stephens (2011). The real data experiment had n=3 895, p=1 051 811.

- Could you describe more about the properties of the implied marginal prior? Now you write that it gets more concentrated, but I'm interested how the tail shape behaves or how would the implied marginal prior on the amount of shrinkage look like (cf. horseshoe prior paper)

- In the prior for R^2, the first parameter is K/2 and the second is eta. Information about the location of R^2 is used to choose eta. How is the amount of prior information controlled (weakly informative vs strong information)? If you think it is not needed, it would helpfull to comment anyway, why there is no another parameter for controlling how strong the prior information is about specific location of R^2.

- In the experiment you write "R^2 should be fairly small". How did you decide 0.2 is good value for fairly small? Why not 0.1 or 0.3? Is the result sensitive to this?

Aki

On Thursday, March 24, 2016 at 1:30:43 AM UTC+2, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> The stan_lm function in rstanarm implements a linear model with regularizing priors driven by prior beliefs about the R^2. This has been confusing to many users and pretty much everyone except for Ben (who had the idea for this cool prior). In light of the confusion, I've written a rough draft of a paper about the prior and I would very much appreciate some feedback. The latest version is attached as a pdf. You can also find the pdf as well as the raw .tex file and R code for the graphics on GitHub in my R2prior repository.
>
>
> The paper is pretty short (9 pages or so) so it should be a quick read.
>
>
> Thanks,
>
>
> Jonah

On Monday, March 28, 2016 at 3:27:02 PM UTC-4, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> - Could you describe more about the properties of the implied marginal prior? Now you write that it gets more concentrated, but I'm interested how the tail shape behaves or how would the implied marginal prior on the amount of shrinkage look like (cf. horseshoe prior paper)

For an unknown correlation matrix among the K -1 predictors (the paper / vignette redefines this as K predictors), the 1-dimensional PDF of any standardized coefficient is "known" to be

which is not very intuitive. The characteristic function is also known and real (so the odd moments are zero if they exist) so

We also know the characteristic function (but not the density) of the full-conditional distribution, which may provide some intuition

> - In the prior for R^2, the first parameter is K/2 and the second is eta. Information about the location of R^2 is used to choose eta. How is the amount of prior information controlled (weakly informative vs strong information)? If you think it is not needed, it would helpfull to comment anyway, why there is no another parameter for controlling how strong the prior information is about specific location of R^2.

Yeah, I started out thinking about the traditional case where the number of observations was large relative to a fixed number of predictors, and you get this Beta(K/2, eta) prior on the R^2. But more generally K could be the rank of the design matrix in the case where there are more predictors than observations or K could even be the expected number of non-zero coefficients. We haven't worked out the case yet where there are more predictors than observations.

> - In the experiment you write "R^2 should be fairly small". How did you decide 0.2 is good value for fairly small? Why not 0.1 or 0.3? Is the result sensitive to this?

The coefficients are a bit sensitive but mostly because there are something like 25 observations and 12 parameters. I don't think the estimate of the average treatment effect is very sensitive to this. In general, the data are informative about the R^2.

Thanks,
Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
messages.body_plain:
I think it might help to add a discussion of the relation between
quantiles and (inverse) CDFs.  You can compute the marginal CDF
of any parameter theta at point x conditioned on some data y as

  F_theta(x) = Pr[theta > x | y] = E[I[theta > x] | y]

But I don't know how to compute quantiles directly as expectations.

And what can I do if one of my variables has a marginal posterior
that's Cauchy?  I don't think I can even properly marginalize it out,
or will there be cases where

  INT f(alpha) * Cauchy(alpha | 0, 1) d.alpha

converges, even though

  INT alpha * Cauchy(alpha | 0, 1) d.alpha

doesn't?  That must be the case if in the posterior some of the
other variables are not Cauchy.  (I realize these are going to
be problematic for NUTS, but that's a different issue.)

- Bob

> On Mar 27, 2016, at 5:05 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
>
> I really enjoyed reading the text, although I'm biased as I'm familiar
> with the topic. I guess many of my master level students would have
> difficulties but those same have have difficulties with BDA, too. I'll
> give this to some of my more advanced students to read, too.  Overall
> it's an excellent overview (or beginning of such overview) and answers
> many FAQs in the Stan users list.
>
> One specific comment. You write
> "Consequently the small world is equivalent to a probability distribution over the measurements space conditioned on the small world,
> ...
> This conditional probability distribution is also known as the likelihood."
>
> p(d|theta) as a function of d is conditional probability distribution.
>
> p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which
> is not a probability distribution. Sometimes it's proportional to a
> probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required
> to make it possible to normalise the posterior.
>
> I think it is important to make this distinction to have a different
> name for p(d|theta) and L(d|theta), but also because the models are
> often described as generative models using conditional probability
> distributions (observation models), but in Stan we often also write
> some terms of log likelihood directly (e.g. for models with
> censoring). I think that the new notation is also making it more
> explicit that we are making statements about parameters theta.
>
> Aki
>
>
>
> Friday, March 18, 2016 at 1:47:10 AM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> One of the common problems that we keep running into is that
>> everyone has different, and usually incomplete, understandings
>> of probability.  Of course probability theory is relatively abstract
>> and we’re not going to be able to teach it to those without
>> reasonable math backgrounds: in that case the approaches
>> of McElreath and Kruschke are probably best.  What doesn’t
>> exist in the literature is an introductory treatment of probability
>> theory and inference that goes into all of the technical details
>> for those who do have a reasonable math background.  I’m
>> talking about concepts like concentration of measure, the
>> difference between probability, probability mass functions,
>> and probability density function.
>>
>> Anyways, I think we’re going to need a treatment like that
>> in the Stan manual going forward, and this is my best
>> attempt at an initial draft, https://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro/blob/master/stan_intro.pdf.
>> Conditioned on a familiarity with calculus everything should,
>> hopefully, be self-contained and well-defined.
>>
>> The inference section is still a little bit in flux, but I’m really
>> happy about the general organization of the probability sections.
>> That said, I’m sure there are many topics that unclear or
>> too hastily introduced or could use more examples to build
>> intuition, so let me have it.  Either here on the list or via an
>> issue/PR.  Otherwise let me know what you think.
>

messages.subject_clean: buffering output [was [stan-users] RStan multiple parallel instances ...]
messages.body_plain:
Should we be thinking about some kind of buffering mechanism
for the output that doesn't involve files?  Network file
systems can have high latency, which would really benefit from
buffering if the output isn't needed online.

I'm thinking we could build that functionality into specialized
writer filters (basically writer classes that hold references to
other writers).

- Bob

> > Hi, sorry for the delay in getting back to this topic. There is a command in Stata to install from a company-approved database of commands which is run by Kit Baum at Boston College, so to get StataStan, our users would most likely type:

> > net install statastan, from("http://mc-stan.org/statastan")
> >

> >
> > Both of these work with the current arrangement! But the unstable one needs some work. Sorry about the sparkly blue comic sans. I had no idea it would look so awful! All of this github pages stuff is new for me, and the last week or two have been too hectic to get to grips with it. messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] buffering output [was [stan-users] RStan multiple parallel instances ...]
messages.body_plain:
We're (and by that I mean someone other than me) is working on protocol
buffer support.  The new writer framework should make buffering very
easy to implement.

- Bob

> On Mar 31, 2016, at 10:18 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> We are using Stan in a cluster with network attached storage. And YES, buffering stuff sounds great if this make IO faster in this setting. Moreover, straight binary output or at least compression would be amazing.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Thursday, March 31, 2016 at 2:12:18 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Should we be thinking about some kind of buffering mechanism
>> for the output that doesn't involve files?  Network file
>> systems can have high latency, which would really benefit from
>> buffering if the output isn't needed online.
>>
>> I'm thinking we could build that functionality into specialized
>> writer filters (basically writer classes that hold references to
>> other writers).
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> Begin forwarded message:
>>>
>>>
>>> cool, I'll give that a try.
>>>
>>> with regards to local vs network storage, is there a way to change the
>>> path for the rda file so I'm not writing that to an NFS? and is there
>>> any file system swapping I should be worried about with the draws?
>>> (i.e. I'm trying to reduce how much I hit the network drive.)
>>>

messages.body_plain: I wrote and tested a protocol buffers binary writer that's a drop in replacement for the file writer in cmdstan.  The main issue with going further down that road is that we don't have an agreed on output format and I don't want to push it forward and then have to rewrite everything when we agree on a format.
